summary: Documents the protocols Microsoft Windows 2000 uses for changing and setting Kerberos passwords. The change-password protocol interoperates with the original Kerberos one and carries the new password in a KRB_PRIV message. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Here is how one company's computers ask the login system to change a password, written down so others can make their programs work the same way.

questions: how to change kerberos password on windows 2000
subtitle: Windows 2000 protocols for Kerberos password changes and administrative password setting.

tldr.problem: Windows 2000 systems need a way for users to change their Kerberos passwords, and for administrators to set passwords for new accounts. The original Kerberos change-password protocol does not support password setting.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies request-reply protocols on UDP and TCP port 464 that wrap Kerberos authentication (AP-REQ) and encrypted password data (KRB-PRIV) to allow secure password change and set operations.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can now set initial passwords for new users, and users can change their passwords while maintaining interoperability with standard Kerberos change-password.

today: RFC 3244 documents Windows 2000 Kerberos password protocols informally. The specifications are still used in Windows environments for password management. For new deployments, administrators should consult current Windows and Kerberos documentation.

sections.title: Kerberos Password Management
sections.content:
Kerberos is a network authentication system where a server (the Key Distribution Center, or KDC) stores user passwords and issues credentials to prove identity. When a user logs in or changes their password, the KDC is involved.

RFC 3244 documents how Microsoft Windows 2000 implements password change and set operations. The change-password protocol is compatible with the original Kerberos protocol but extends it with a new feature: password setting, where an administrator can assign a password to a newly created account without the user having to authenticate first.
sections.plainLanguage: Kerberos is a login system. Users need to change their passwords sometimes. This RFC explains how Windows does it so other systems can understand the same language.

sections.title: Request and Reply Message Structure
sections.content:
The protocol uses UDP port 464 and TCP port 464. Messages have a 4-octet header for TCP showing message length. All 16-bit fields are big-endian.

A request message contains: a 2-byte message length, a 2-byte protocol version (hex 0xff80), a 2-byte AP-REQ length, the AP-REQ data (Kerberos authentication), and a KRB-PRIV message (encrypted with a subsession key from the AP-REQ authenticator) holding the new password in an ASN.1 structure with fields for the new password, an optional target principal name, and optional target realm.

A reply message has: message length, protocol version (0x0001), AP-REP length, the AP-REP response, and a KRB-PRIV message (or KRB-ERROR if decoding failed) with a result code and optional result string in UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: A request says 'change my password' and proves who you are with Kerberos magic, then whispers the new password in an encrypted box. The reply says 'done' or explains what went wrong.

sections.title: Protocol Operation and Result Codes
sections.content:
When changing a password, the client sends a request with the new password encrypted inside the KRB-PRIV message using a subsession key. The server verifies the AP-REQ message, checks if the client is authorized to change the password (either their own or another principal's if specified in targname), and applies local password policy checks.

The server responds with result codes: 0x0000 for success, 0x0005 for authorization denied, 0x0006 for unsupported protocol version, 0x0007 if the initial flag is required but not set, and others for various errors. The reply may include a UTF-8 text message describing the result, such as password policy feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks your permission, follows password rules, and tells you 'okay' or why it refused—like 'that password is too weak'.

sections.title: Password Setting for New Accounts
sections.content:
The Windows 2000 extension allows administrators to set a password for a newly created account. The client includes a targname field in the request to specify which principal's password to set. The server checks if the client is authorized as an administrator.

Unlike the original change-password protocol, password setting does not require the initial flag to be set in the Kerberos service ticket. This lets an administrator (who may not have the user's credentials) set a password that the new user can use to log in. The server generates appropriate key types from the password and stores them in the KDC database.
sections.plainLanguage: Admins can use this to give new employees their first password without needing to log in as the employee first.

sections.title: Password Policies and Credential Protection
sections.content:
The RFC requires that password policies be enforced to prevent weak passwords vulnerable to guessing attacks. The new password string in the request is encrypted under the subsession key derived from mutual Kerberos authentication, so it is protected in transit.

Administrators authorized to set other users' passwords are highly trusted and must carefully protect their own credentials. The RFC also notes that applications using Kerberos failover must be aware of security state (authentication, cached ciphertext for block ciphers): when a user's connection fails over to another server, that security state may need to be re-established. This is an application design concern, not handled by the protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Passwords must be hard to guess. The secret is encrypted when sent. Admins are powerful and must keep their own passwords safe.
